sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

Introduction In the world of Harry Potter, Platform 9¾ allows travelers to pass through solid wall and enter another world [36]. In reality, however, wall cannot be crossed because its solid. Todays world models [7, 8, 15, 18, 35, 38, 43, 48, 51, 53] may still behave as if every wall were Platform 9¾. As shown in Fig. 1, when commanded to move into wall, five of the six generators we evaluate pass through it, while the remaining one moves against the users command. These failures reveal that current world models struggle to enforce the non-penetration constraint. The underlying principle, however, is not new. In computer graphics, non-penetration requires that solid objects cannot occupy the same space [4]. Simulators and game engines have long enforced this constraint through collision detection and collision response [25]. They detect collisions and adjust the motion to prevent penetration while preserving the intended movement as much as possible. Unfortunately, this mechanism is missing from todays video world models. Basically, they are designed to follow user commands, whether camera poses [8, 15, 38, 48, 53] or key inputs [51], without checking whether the motion is physically possible. Since their training videos rarely, if ever, show command blocked by wall, such command is likely out of distribution. As result, cameras may pass through walls, or obstacles simply disappear. Worse still, existing benchmarks largely use collision-free trajectories, making it difficult to evaluate how well world models handle non-penetration [14, 45, 46, 49]. To prevent such failures, two straightforward solutions seem promising at first glance. The first is to simply prompt the model to stop or slide along obstacles. However, we find that such prompts have little effect on penetration. The second is to use an external depth estimator [21, 30] to detect obstacles and stop unsafe motions. While effective, this requires post-hoc processing with an additional network for every generated frame. Moreover, stopping alone may In that sense, both sacrifice the users intended motion. methods have their own limitations. Surprisingly, we find that the generator itself already contains information needed to prevent penetration. Prior studies have shown that video diffusion models encode 3D structure and physical plausibility [9, 13, 50]. We find that this knowledge extends to predicting penetration. Specifically, the hidden states of diffusion transformer (DiT) can predict whether commanded action will cause penetration, even before the next video chunk is generated. In short, the generator already knows where its walls are, but its output fails to act on that knowledge. Building on this observation, we introduce NoPeWorld, lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration in video world models. The rough idea is that rather than relying on external tools, we directly read the generators hidden states to detect unsafe actions  (Fig. 2)  . Specifically, we train small prediction head on frozen DiT to predict collision risks and distances to obstacles. The head is trained using ground-truth distance and collision labels from Unreal Engine simulations. During inference, unsafe motions are replaced with safe alternatives that best preserve the users intent, while safe motions remain unchanged. We achieve this through two detection modes. In collision mode, the head reads the initial denoising features of the current chunk to detect potential penetration. In prediction mode, it uses features from the previous chunk to predict penetration in the upcoming chunk. new task, of course, requires new benchmark. To evaluate this, we introduce NoPeBench, benchmark that deliberately challenges world models with obstacles (Sec. 4.1). It consists of three levels of tasks. Task 1 evaluates, on ground-truth histories, whether method keeps safe commands and corrects those that would penetrate. Task 2 evaluates whether generated videos respect non-penetration using the ground-truth geometry of scenes from UnrealZoo [55]. Task 3 tests generalization to open-domain scenes using vision-language model (VLM) as judges. Our experiments show that NoPeWorld robustly detects and prevents penetration across diverse video world models. On LingBot-World 2.0 [15], NoPeWorld intercepts nearly all unsafe commands (Tab. 3), which cuts violations from 89% to 4% and lifts the Safe-Intent Score, zero for any video with violation, from near zero to about half (Sec. 4.4 and Tab. 4). Moreover, the heads transfer without retraining: trained only on first-person walks through static scenes from UnrealZoo, they reduce Task 3 violations on all six generators, on open-domain imagery, from third-person viewpoint, and around moving obstacles. Our contributions are fourfold. (i) Problem: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to study the problem of penetration prevention in video world models. (ii) Method: We introduce NoPeWorld, which detects collisions by probing the hidden states of frozen DiT and replaces unsafe motions with the safe motion that best preserves the users intent. (iii) Insights: We show that frozen world generators encode collision information even before future frames are generated (Sec. 5.1). Such collision awareness can be exploited across visual domains, camera viewpoints, and moving obstacles without retraining. (iv) Benchmark: We collect new benchmark called NoPeBench. It evaluates whether video world models can prevent penetration when given commands that would otherwise lead to collisions. 2. Related work Interactive video world models. Interactive video generation has progressed from early action-conditioned predictors [2, 7, 43] to diffusion transformers [28, 41] that denoise video chunk by chunk under camera-pose or keystroke con2 Figure 2. NoPeWorld. Training: every candidate motion is swept through Unreals true geometry (top view) and labelled; the head predicts the labels from the frozen DiTs states (outlined: keeping the input). Because actions condition denoising in an open loop without scene geometry, these models do not explicitly enforce collision constraints [30]. Prompting with obstacle descriptions fails to prevent clipping, while guarding decoded frames with an external depth estimator [21, 30] requires VAE decoding and auxiliary 3D inference at every chunk and only halts motion (Secs. 4.3 and 5.3). NoPeWorld instead keeps the generator frozen and enforces collision-aware control directly inside the DiT loop (Sec. 3). Collision handling in computer graphics. Computer graphics and mechanics have enforced solid non-penetration since the 1980s through collision impulses [16, 25], unilateral contact constraints [4, 5, 22, 23, 26, 37], and penalty potentials [42], later extended to continuous swept collision detection against thin-wall tunnelling [33] and intersectionfree solvers [19]. All of these methods require explicit 3D geometry and solve contact mechanics on known surfaces. Rather than simulating contact forces, we adapt two kinematic principles, continuous swept clearance and frictionless collide-and-slide projection (Sec. 3.1), to video generator that stores no geometry, replacing unsafe commands with admissible stops or wall slides. Internal representations of diffusion models. Intermediate features of image and video diffusion models capture semantic correspondence, depth, and 3D structure beyond surface appearance [6, 9, 40, 50]. Recent studies probe hidden states [1] on intuitive-physics tasks [34] to show that video DiTs encode physical plausibility offline even when generated frames violate it [13], or train verifier on frozen DiT features to select among multiple sampled trajectories [39]. Consistent with this view, we find that frozen DiT states already predict upcoming obstacle contact before the next chunk is synthesized, whereas the same readout on VAE latents or decoded pixels falls short (Sec. 5.1). Rather than offline probing or multi-sample rejection after generation, NoPeWorld queries frozen DiT tokens with lightweight cross-attention head (Sec. 3.2) to score and replace unsafe actions prior to chunk synthesis (Sec. 3.3). World model benchmarks. Physical video benchmarks [3, 24, 27] evaluate passive clips without user control, whereas interactive world-model benchmarks [14, 4547, 49, 52] focus on visual quality, memory, and action following along open paths: WorldMark [46] removes wall-blocked trajectories, WBench [49] scores clipping as one VLM rubric item along mostly unobstructed routes (Sec. 4.1), and WorldRoamBench [45] tests 58 clipping and 14 collision cases with VLMs. To evaluate non-penetration directly, NoPeBench (Sec. 4.1) commands every test route into an obstacle alongside open-path controls across teacher-forced (Task 1), closed-loop (Task 2), and open-domain (Task 3) settings, pairing verified 3D reconstruction [44] and humanvalidated VLM judges with hard-gated Safe-Intent Score inspired by NAVSIM [10] (Sec. 4.2). 3. Experiments 4.1. NoPeBench NoPeBench  (Fig. 3)  tests whether world model enforces non-penetration without overriding safe user intent. Existing interactive benchmarks largely steer around obstacles: in WBench [49], scripted trajectories drive into visible obstacle in only 13 of 158 navigation cases by our count, recording clipping passively rather than testing contact. In NoPeBench every test command drives into solid obstacle, and 50 unobstructed open-path routes check against unnecessary intervention, so both clipping and needless halting are penalized. All scenes, assets, and images are disjoint from training and validation (Sec. S1.1). To separate perception from rollout drift and domain shift, NoPeBench has three progressive tasks. Task 1 isolates single-step decisions from generation drift: it replays groundtruth histories by teacher forcing on 100 collision routes in 32 held-out scenes from UnrealZoo [55] and records the action chosen at each chunk. Task 2 runs 5 of obstaclebound commands in closed loop on the same routes, from pre-contact hand-off on true frames. Task 3 starts from single open-domain image without history (131 obstaclebound images: 81 from WBench with static obstacles and 50 with moving ones, in first and third person). 4.2. Relative 8 to the 53.7 raw route, Pred adds about 1%, Coll 18% and External depth 27%. 6. Conclusion Video world models inhabit world where walls are optional. We formulated non-penetration for generators without geometry, requiring that the depicted trajectory never penetrate an obstacle and that no obstacle be erased, and introduced NoPeBench to evaluate it on ground-truth 3D geometry and on open-domain scenes. Rather than rely on external perception, NoPeWorld resolves collisions from within: because frozen DiT already encodes impending contact before it synthesizes pixels, small head suffices for collision detection and response, and transfers without retraining to new domains, viewpoints, and moving obstacles. Across six frozen generators, it cuts violations from 74% to 16%. Solid boundaries are only the first step; the frontier ahead is contact that pushes, carries, and shatters objects.

Training and validation Each head trains online while the frozen generator replays the training videos with their true latents and poses, updating on the tapped tokens of each decision state as they are computed.
